reason: Survives. I went at the plate number, which is the only soft spot a proverb citation has, and it held. Wikisource's transcription of copy D, plate 7 (Page:The_Marriage_of_Heaven_and_Hell_-_copy_D.djvu/7) opens mid-word with “roding fires he wrote the following sentence”, the tail of the Memorable Fancy, and closes with “Shame is Prides cloke.” The Proverbs of Hell therefore begin on plate 7 and plate 7 carries them as far as that line, so the proverb is on plate 7 as claimed. Reading the Proverbs in order from the Wikisource text of the whole work, this is the tenth: In seed time learn; Drive your cart; The road of excess; Prudence is a rich ugly old maid; He who desires but acts not; The cut worm; Dip him in the river; A fool sees not the same tree; He whose face gives no light; then “Eternity is in love with the productions of time.” Wording and terminal stop match exactly, and there is no rival rendering to drift from since Blake wrote in English and engraved it himself. Attribution is not in dispute and the line is not on the misattribution list. No character speaks it, so no speaker is owed. Shipped.js: not shipped, no near miss, Blake at 0 of 3, not banned. In scope: pre-2000, not scripture, not an anonymous proverb but an authored one inside a named work, nothing needing a warning. Source line leads with the name, 80 characters, no dash; 1790 is the title page date. Tag Poetry is defensible for an illuminated prophetic book even though the proverbs themselves are set as prose, and rule 7 is satisfied because the line is not broken. One inaccuracy in the verifier's evidence, not in the citation: plate 7 does not stop at “If the fool would persist in his folly”, it runs on through “Folly is the cloke of knavery” to “Shame is Prides cloke.” The claim that matters, that the proverb falls on plate 7, I confirmed independently.
